bibliographic.title: Evaluation of Off-the-Ball Actions in Soccer
bibliographic.venue: Statistica Applicata — Italian Journal of Applied Statistics, (2)

scope.rationale: The paper develops an automatic, quantitative metric (defensive anticipation) for evaluating off-the-ball defensive actions in soccer, using machine learning over player tracking data. This is squarely within the action-valuation / off-ball-action literature.

model.name: Defensive Anticipation Metric (P-score)
inputs: distance of the player to the ball (1-dim)
distance of the player to offensive goal (1-dim)
angle of the player to offensive goal (1-dim)
distance of the player to goalkeeper (1-dim)
indicator for the player on offensive or defensive side of the field (1-dim)
indicator for player belonging to the home or road team (1-dim)
seconds remaining in the half of the game (1-dim)
seconds remaining in the full game (1-dim)

for each of the player's three nearest teammates: location (2-dim), velocity (2-dim), distance of the player to teammate (1-dim), distance of the ball to teammate (1-dim), relative angle of the teammate to the player of interest (1-dim)

for each of the player's three nearest opponents: location (2-dim), velocity (2-dim), distance of the player to opponent (1-dim), distance of the ball to opponent (1-dim), expected possession value EPV of opponent (1-dim), relative angle of the opponent to the player of interest (1-dim)
model.target: Two-dimensional velocity vector (y1, y2) — directional components — of a defensive player in a given spatio-temporal situation; derived metric p compares observed vs predicted velocity to score defensive anticipation.
model.architecture: Two LightGBM gradient-boosted tree models (one per velocity component, x and y), trained over a 61-dimensional covariate vector built from tracking data. Per-instance score p is a closed-form projection (Eq. 1) of the observed velocity onto the predicted velocity direction; season-long P-score is the mean of p across instances scaled by 100% (Eq. 2).
model.temporal_horizon: next instant (predict velocity at time t given state, with Delta = 0.5 seconds prior velocity covariate; analysis stepped every epsilon = 1 second)

data.provider: Shandong Luneng Taishan FC (CSL data provided by Daniel Stenz)

metrics: mean absolute error of 0.319 m/sec in the x-coordinate velocity
mean absolute error of 0.398 m/sec in the y-coordinate velocity
correlation r ≈ 0.9 between predicted speed at time t and actual speed at time t-Delta (with Delta = 0.5 seconds)
rank consistency of P-score across even vs odd weeks (Table 1: identical ranks for top-10 Shandong Luneng players)
Pearson correlation between P-score and fouls = 0.60
Pearson correlation between P-score and successful tackles = 0.65
Pearson correlation between P-score and interceptions = 0.49
Leaguewise scatterplot correlation R = 0.32 (interceptions per game) and R = 0.29 (tackles won per game)
evaluation.splits: 20-week season partitioned into training (even weeks 2,4,...,20) and test (odd weeks 1,3,...,19); leave-one-week-out cross validation used to select LightGBM tuning parameters. Split is by week rather than strictly by match; potential within-week leakage not discussed.

claims.statement: Using roughly four million spatio-temporal instances, the LightGBM models predict the two-dimensional velocity vector of a defensive player; the fitted model provides a mean absolute error of 0.319 m/sec in the x-coordinate velocity and 0.398 m/sec in the y-coordinate velocity.
The tuning parameter Delta = 0.5 seconds was selected such that the correlation between predicted speed at time t and actual speed at time t-Delta is approximately r = 0.9 (Figure 1).

The 2019 CSL dataset consists of 237 regular season matches (from a potential 240; 3 missing) across 16 teams, with tracking data recorded every 1/10th of a second (roughly one million rows per match across 7 variables).
The design matrix used for model training contained 3,770,289 rows and required just under 100 hours of computation on a laptop computer; LightGBM training itself required approximately 1.5 hours.

Observations with predicted speed less than the threshold of 0.20 m/sec (0.72 km/hour) were removed from the metric; in the test dataset, 1.8% of observations were removed due to the threshold constraint.

Reliability: for the 10 Shandong Luneng players with N > 10,000 instances in both even and odd weeks of 2019, the rankings produced by the defensive anticipation metric are identical across the two sets of weeks.
Validity: correlations between the P-score and season-long aggression statistics for the 10 Shandong Luneng players are 0.60 (fouls), 0.65 (successful tackles) and 0.49 (interceptions).
League-wide, for all CSL players with at least 500 minutes played in 2019, scatterplots relate P to interceptions per game (R = 0.32) and tackles won per game (R = 0.29).

Averaged across all CSL players in 10-minute intervals, P decreases as the match progresses, with a sharp drop after the 70th minute; this conforms to the common-sense expectation that defensive anticipation declines as players tire.
Among CSL players with regular minutes, the two highest P-scores are Chang Feiya of Wuhan Zall (P = 5.71) and Yang Shiyuan of Shanghai SIPG (P = 5.33).

Validity by playing position: among all 438 outfield CSL players (n = 79 wide midfielders, n = 77 wide defenders, n = 86 forwards, n = 110 central midfielders, n = 86 central defenders), there is little difference in P across playing positions; central midfielders have slightly larger values on average and forwards exhibit greater variability (Figure 4).

limitations: There is no gold standard for 'defensive anticipation' to validate against; the authors note that they 'do not know with certainty which players play with more and less defensive anticipation'.

The approach considers off-the-ball actions only for defensive players (i.e. when the player's team does not have possession); offensive off-ball movement is acknowledged as a more challenging future-research direction because there are multiple potential paths offensive players may choose.
Inferences are specific to the 2019 CSL season, although the methods are claimed to be applicable to any league with tracking data.
Three of the 240 potential regular-season matches are missing from the dataset.
open_questions: Investigating alternative predictive models beyond LightGBM for predicting average player movement.

Extending the framework to evaluate off-the-ball actions for players on the team in possession (offensive off-ball movement), which is harder because there are more viable options for offensive players.
